samples.task_summary: Predict whether an NHANES participant has high cholesterol / has been told they have high cholesterol using features likely to generalize across benchmark domain shifts.

scores.rationale: Hypertension is a strong cardiometabolic correlate of dyslipidemia and should remain predictive across domains.
Prediabetes reflects metabolic dysfunction linked to abnormal cholesterol and is likely fairly stable across settings.
Diabetes is a robust risk factor for dyslipidemia and should generalize well as a semantically related comorbidity.
Dialysis indicates severe kidney disease that can affect lipids, but it is rare and may be unstable due to treatment-related selection.
Kidney disease has some physiological association with lipid abnormalities, though weaker and less direct than core metabolic features.
Psoriasis has only a modest indirect association with cardiometabolic risk and is unlikely to be a strong stable marginal predictor.
Arthritis may correlate through age and inflammation, but much of its signal is likely indirect and redundant.
Survey year is primarily a domain identifier and risks exploiting temporal prevalence or measurement shifts rather than stable biology.
Country of birth may proxy lifestyle or access differences but is a demographic shortcut with questionable transportability.
Education captures socioeconomic patterns affecting diet, care access, and diagnosis, but it is partly a brittle social proxy.
Age is one of the most stable and consistently strong predictors of high cholesterol prevalence and diagnosis.
Sex/gender has biologically grounded differences in lipid profiles, though effect size is moderate and can vary by age.
Marital status is mostly an indirect social proxy and likely less stable for out-of-distribution generalization.

Survey year is primarily a domain indicator and risks exploiting temporal shifts rather than stable disease mechanisms.
Country of birth may proxy lifestyle or access differences but is a demographic shortcut with limited stable causal relevance.
Education can capture socioeconomic influences on diet and care, but it is indirect and potentially domain-sensitive.
